discoveries.name: Where the Record Starts

levels.entry: The archive is four hundred and eleven years old and complete. I have never seen anything like it.
Four hundred and eleven years ago is the Shattering. The record begins the year the world broke.
Which is reasonable -- that is when they started measuring. It is also the one year you would least want as your first.
Every normal in these volumes is a post-Shattering normal. The rainfall they call average, the riverflow they call standard, the coastline they call the coastline.

Vessa knows. She has known for some time and has not been able to say it in a form the halls would accept, because the form the halls accept is a measurement, and you cannot measure a thing you were not there for.
The plateau is covered in evidence from before: the terraces, the quarry section, the marks on the stones, the herders' years. None of it is a measurement, so none of it is in the archive.
The archive is not wrong. It is a perfect record of the wound, kept by careful people who mistook it for the body.

discoveries.notes: The thesis. Seven rungs, and gated on two other discoveries so it cannot be reached by walking into the building -- the player has to bring the plateau's evidence in with them. Deliberately sympathetic to the University in the last line.

discoveries.name: The Millet They Say Is Poison

levels.entry: A hardy millet grows on the wet ground below the spring. The archive lists it as toxic to stock and to people.
Marn's household eats it. Has always eaten it. Loses an animal to it about once a year and considers this normal.
They soak it two days in running water and throw the first water away. Untreated, it is exactly as toxic as the archive says.
The animals they lose are the ones that get into the standing crop. The archive tested the plant; the herders solved the food. Both of them stopped there.
Soaking works because the thing in it is water-soluble and sits in the husk. Which means threshing first and soaking after wastes a day and half the effect.

discoveries.notes: Botany, and the one where the player materially improves something rather than merely understanding it. Neither party is wrong here -- both are incompletely right, which is the map's thesis in miniature.

discoveries.name: Somebody Came Back For It
discoveries.subject: faction_mask_family

levels.entry: The undercroft is not one room. There is a second, behind the west wall, and the wall is a wall on one side only.
It was closed from the outside and it was closed in a hurry -- the facing stones are the right stones, put back in the wrong order.
Inside there is a shelf at shoulder height, cut for something specific, and empty. It is the same height as the niche in the stair, and it is the same shape.

So the thing that stood in the stair was brought down here and put behind a wall. Not hidden from thieves -- a thief does not rebuild the wall behind him -- hidden from something that was already inside the building.
There is soot on the shelf and none anywhere else. Something burned in a room with no chimney, which is a thing you do once and quickly.
The mortar is post-collapse. Whatever happened here happened after the tower sat down, which is to say the city was already broken and somebody came back into it for this.

The shelf is empty too. Whoever sealed the room came back and took it, and I cannot say who, or when, or whether it was the same hands. Uvai. A thing remembered, which is what the Kia call the part of a story that outlasts the people in it -- and this is the shape of one with the middle gone.

discoveries.notes:
The mask thread, extending `discovery_mask_niche` without resolving it. Canon knows the answer -- `event_tendua_crisis` and `event_mask_retrieval` name Nila, Asha, iKnaya and Varna -- and none of those names appears here, on purpose: who took it should stay unanswered, and `lint_story.py` now enforces that against the cast list rather than trusting it. The niche's own note says who took the mask 'should stay unanswered for a long time; the diary needs entries the player cannot finish', and this is written to that constraint rather than around it.

What Varuna can reach is the *event*: a chamber, opened and closed in a hurry, something burned, a shelf cut for the thing the stair niche also held, and mortar that dates it after the collapse. What he cannot reach is a person. The last rung says so out loud, which is the honest end of an archaeological reading and a better entry than a solved case.

Every prerequisite is on Lothal. `word_kia_uvai` comes from Thrali after `discovery_ghost_mangrove_channel`, which this also requires and which opens the flooded undercroft in the first place -- so the word is always gettable before this chain needs it. That ordering is deliberate: the two-bar trap is requiring a word an NPC only gives once the requiring chain is already finished.

discoveries.name: The Stair Above the Rock

levels.entry: A cut stair climbs the scarp. Above the scarp it continues. There is nothing under the upper flights.
It is the same stone and the same cut. Whoever made the lower part made the upper part, or copied it exactly.
The wear is on the middle of the treads, all the way up, including the steps with no rock beneath them. Something used them enough to wear them.
On a clear night you can see how far it goes, and it does not stop where the cloud stops.
The lift on the scarp is real and it is nowhere near enough to hold stone. I can describe this exactly and explain none of it, and I have decided that writing it down accurately is the work.

discoveries.notes: Deliberately unresolved. The last rung is the diary refusing to guess, which is the discipline the whole game is about; the sky routes are a later map's problem.

discoveries.name: A Reef in a Square Basin

levels.entry: The water here has corners.
A basin, brick-lined, perhaps two hundred feet on a side. Far too regular to be anything but built.
Lothal's dockyard, which the chronicles describe and which nobody has seen dry in living memory.
The sluice is silted shut. It has been a closed pool since the Shattering, and everything in it has been in it that whole time.

discoveries.notes: Archaeology that unlocks two other chains. Being a closed system is what makes it evidence for both the salt and the lurker.

discoveries.name: One Bird, Two Entries

levels.entry: The archive lists a grey scarp-bird twice, under two names, catalogued sixty years apart.
The descriptions differ in exactly one respect: the later one is larger and has a heavier bill.
Both entries are careful. Both are signed. Neither cites the other, which means the second observer did not know the first entry existed.
In the field they are one bird. The heavy-billed ones are the old ones -- the bill keeps growing, and a bird that lives thirty years ends up looking like a different species.
Marn's people have one word for it and a second word for an old one, which is not two species either. They have been more accurate than the archive for as long as the archive has existed.
Two entries, one bird, and no mechanism anywhere in the University for noticing. Nobody rereads the stacks. There is no reason to, if you believe the record is a record.

discoveries.notes: The self-referential one: this is the binomial-contradiction problem the two repos actually had, put in the fiction. Resolves without villainy -- the failure is structural, not personal.

discoveries.name: How the Air Stands

levels.entry: The cloud on the scarp is not weather passing. It sits in one place and the weather goes through it.
Warm air off the plain hits the black rock and is turned straight up. The cloud is where it cools, and the scarp holds it there.
It is strongest in the afternoon and it fails at night, and when it fails the cloud falls down the scarp in one piece.
Standing in it, the lift is enough to take a hat and keep it. Not a metaphor -- I lost one and watched it go up.

discoveries.notes: The mundane half of the anomaly, and the prerequisite for the interesting half. Establishes real physics on the scarp so that what the stair does cannot be explained by it.

discoveries.name: Something Is Doing Well Here

levels.entry: The seaward orchard rows are dead of salt. In among them something is thriving that I do not recognise.
Thick leaf, no wax, and it is fruiting in the shade of dead trees in the wrong season.
It is not salt-tolerant, it is salt-indifferent -- the soil chemistry does not appear to be a variable for it at all.
Nothing eats it. Not the goats, not the insects, not the rot. In a delta, that is a stranger fact than the leaf shape.
It is spreading at about a pace a year, along the dead rows, and no farmer here is worried because it grows where nothing grows.
Which is the mistake. It is not filling ground nothing wanted. It is making ground that nothing else can use, and it is doing it slowly enough that nobody has thought to measure.

discoveries.notes: An establishment event in progress, which is slower and worse than a monster. The last rung is the only place on this map where the player knows something the locals do not.

discoveries.name: What the Gate Keeps Time With

levels.entry: There is a doorway in the court that people walk around rather than through. Nobody has told me not to. I have not.
It is not always doing anything. Most of the day it is a doorway in a wall.
In mist it is doing something. The air on the far side is a different air -- warmer, and it smells of stone rather than salt.
Not the tide — there has not been a tide here in sixty years — and not the hour. I sat the stair for three days with a slate and the only thing that matches is the mist.
Which is backwards. Mist is water in air; it does not open anything. Unless the mist and the opening are both downstream of a third thing, and I have been watching the wrong one.
Pell says the sweeping is done at mist and always has been. Nobody decided that. It is simply when there is something to sweep.

discoveries.notes: The anomaly, approached as a naturalist would: rule out the tide, rule out the hour, notice the correlation, then notice the correlation is not a cause. Ends honestly short of an explanation. Rewritten when Dwarka was dried out: the sea left rather than the land sinking, so a rung that assumed a live tide now reads against its absence. The chain is stronger for it — a city keeping a tide schedule for water that stopped arriving is a better observation than one keeping it for water that is still there.

discoveries.name: The Pale Mangroves Mark the Channel
discoveries.subject: flora_ghost_mangrove

levels.entry: Mangroves with bark far paler than the others. They seem to be arranged, though that is surely my eye imposing order.
Ghost mangrove, and they are arranged -- in a rough line, with a second line some thirty feet off.
Not planted. They have grown where the water is deep enough to stand and shallow enough to root, which happens to be either side of the old channel.
The Kia have not marked the safe water. The tree has, and the Kia have been reading the tree. Bekh says her grandmother could walk to the shrine at night.
Every pale line in this marsh is a channel that held when the rest silted. They are a map of the delta as it was before the Shattering, drawn by something that did not know it was drawing.
Which means the undercroft of the tower can be reached, if one goes the way the trees go.
Thrali can work the far banks again. It is a morning's walk to show him and it will double the ground his family can fish.

discoveries.notes: Canon already said the ghost mangrove marks safe channels; this is that fact turned into gameplay. Gates the tower undercroft, so botany opens archaeology.

discoveries.name: A Line of Glass

levels.entry: A seam of green-black glass running straight across open sand. Nothing near it is scorched.
Fused sand, and only at the surface — a hand down it is ordinary. Whatever did this was fast enough that the heat never travelled.
It runs true for as far as I walked it, which was most of a morning, and it does not deviate for a dune or a ridge.
It crosses the old harbour floor without a break, and the silt underneath it is unfused. So it happened after the water left, and fast.
I can date it and describe it and I cannot say what it is. I have written down the bearing, which points at the gate court, and I am aware that is not an explanation.

discoveries.notes: Deliberately unresolved, like the Cloud Stair. Its job is to date the ending, not to explain it, and the diary says so. Moved to Dwarka. Rung 3 used to be dated against the fossil channel and is now dated against the harbour floor and the seawalls, which is the same argument with the evidence that survived. The bearing pointing at the gate is new and deliberately unresolved -- its job is still to date the ending, not to explain it.

discoveries.name: The Channel Still Falls
discoveries.subject: settlement_lothal

levels.entry: A stone channel runs into the granary's north wall and stops at a chamber full of silt. It has been dry so long the camp treats it as a wall.
Not dry. There is water in it, moving, under about a foot of silt. It is audible if the marsh is quiet.
The channel drops nearly six feet across the granary's length. That is not drainage -- drainage is laid flat. Something was meant to be turned by it.
The chamber below the drop has a stone floor worn in a circle, and a socket cut in the middle of the circle. Whatever stood in it was taken or rotted.
A mill, and the grain it ground was the red rice from these same chambers. The building is one machine: store, drop, mill, store.
The silt is the whole failure. Six feet of fall is still six feet of fall, and the water never stopped -- it only stopped being able to reach the wheel.
Clear the north chamber and the fall works again. Bekh's people thresh eight acres by hand and the building that would do it for them is standing over their heads.

discoveries.notes: The water half. Nothing is invented: the mill was there, the fall never stopped, and the discovery is that a wall is actually a blocked machine. Requires `discovery_red_rice_survival` twice over -- once to know what was ground here, once because threshing eight acres only matters if the eight acres are sown, which is that chain's own last rung.

discoveries.name: The Wind That Took the Tower Will Fire a Kiln
discoveries.subject: settlement_lothal

levels.entry: The kilns are lit three times a year and never in spring. Uma says spring firings go wrong and nobody knows why.
They do not go wrong. They go cold. A spring firing takes twice the reed and comes out grey.
The wind turns in spring. From the sea eight months of the year, and off the plateau for four -- and the kiln mouths all face the sea.
Kavik knew. The tower's lower courses are pierced on the seaward face and blind on the landward, which is a building arranged around a wind that blows one way.
The same arrangement, and the same mistake. He built for eight months and lost the tower in the fourth. The kilns are losing a firing a year to it.
A kiln mouth is a hole in a wall. It can be moved in a morning, and it only has to be moved once.
Turn the spring kiln to face the plateau and it will fire in a day on half the reed. Uma has cut that reed every spring of her life and burnt it for grey brick.

discoveries.notes: The wind half of the winter chain, and deliberately the smallest. Nothing is built and nothing is invented -- a kiln mouth is moved, because the tower already recorded which way the wind blows and nobody had read it as advice. Requires `discovery_tower_collapse`, which is the archaeology on the same map: the tower is the evidence, not a separate errand.

discoveries.name: Two Mornings a Day

levels.entry: The market opens twice and closes twice, and everyone knows when without being told.
It is the tide, they say, and they are half right: the market still opens on a tide that stopped arriving before most of them were born.
A ledger goes back sixty years of opening times. Nobody kept it for the tide; they kept it for the tolls — which is why the times outlived the water.
Read as a tide record it is better than anything the University has, and it says the high water is arriving later each decade.

discoveries.notes: Local record-keeping outperforming the academy again, and this time entirely by accident -- the ledger was for taxes. Rewritten when Dwarka was dried out: the sea left rather than the land sinking, so a rung that assumed a live tide now reads against its absence. The chain is stronger for it — a city keeping a tide schedule for water that stopped arriving is a better observation than one keeping it for water that is still there.

discoveries.name: The Lurker Waits Where the Water Warms
discoveries.subject: fauna_lothal_marsh_lurker

levels.entry: Something large moved in the pool and I did not see it move.
An enormous salamander, perhaps eight feet, entirely still in the shallow water.
The Lothal Marsh-Lurker, which the old bestiaries have surviving here since the Pleistocene and which I had assumed was a flourish.
It chooses the pools that warm first -- shallow, dark-bottomed, out of the current. It is not hunting so much as banking heat, and the hunting follows.
The warm pools are the old brick chambers. The city built its own predator a habitat and then left.

discoveries.notes: Pure natural history, no help attached. Not every discovery should mend something -- most should just be worth knowing.

discoveries.name: The Empty Niche
discoveries.subject: faction_mask_family

levels.entry: A recess cut into the stair core at shoulder height, lined and finished, and empty.
Cut for something specific: the back is shaped, and the shaping is a face.
A mask niche, of the kind the Mask Family kept. Whatever stood here was taken rather than lost -- the dust line is clean.

discoveries.notes: Left open on purpose. Who took the mask is not answerable in this slice and should stay unanswered for a long time -- the diary needs entries the player cannot finish.

discoveries.name: How Often This Has Happened

levels.entry: The midden is layered like any midden: fish, shell, pot, ash, fish, shell, pot.
There are other layers. Thin ones, of bone I cannot place, and they are not at the top.
I counted nine. The deepest is under a pottery style Sura says her grandmother's grandmother used.
Nine, in four hundred years, and not evenly spaced -- they cluster. Two of them are close enough to be one bad decade.
This is not an event. It is a climate. Dwarka has been dealing with this the whole time it has existed, and has a word for it, and a place to put the remains.

discoveries.notes: Turns the anomaly from an incident into a condition, which is the map's whole argument. The clustering is left unexplained on purpose.

discoveries.name: The Spring Does Not Stay

levels.entry: The archive gives the spring a fixed position, surveyed, with a date. The spring is not in that position.
There are dry basins downslope of it. Someone built them to catch this water, at three different places, at three different times.
On a cold morning the whole line of them steams -- all three, faintly, not just the live one. The rock under them is still wet.
The water is not moving because the hill is moving. It is following a crack, and the crack is opening uphill a little at a time.
Marn's grandmother named a year by it. They have a word for the year the water moved, which means it has moved inside living memory and inside the archive's period, and only one of those noticed.
Three basins, three moves, and the archive's fixed point is simply the position it happened to hold on the day a surveyor walked past.

discoveries.notes: Geography, and the first crack in the archive's authority. The measurement was not wrong -- it was a single measurement of a thing that moves, which is a different and much more forgivable error.

discoveries.name: What Came Up in the Eastern Field

levels.entry: Eight acres that will not grow anything. The camp calls it poisoned.
The soil is good, the water is fresh, and the surface crusts white after a dry week.
Salt, and not sea salt -- there is too much of it and it is coming up rather than blowing in.
Something opened below this field during the Shattering and has been weeping brine into it since. Not a wound one can close.
The same white crust is on the stones at the drowned dockyard, at the same height above the waterline. Whatever opened runs under both.

discoveries.notes: The problem half of the field chain. Stops at connected: understanding the salt is not the same as fixing it, and the fix belongs to the rice.

discoveries.name: The Nine Inches

levels.entry: A pale band in the quarry face, between two courses of basalt. Full of small shells.
The shells are not one kind. Going up through the band they change, and they change in one direction.
At the bottom they are round and thin. At the top, over nine inches, they are ridged and heavy. In between they are both, and neither, and the intermediate ones are the commonest.
Nine inches of ash is not nine inches of time. This is a long slow record laid down between two very fast events.
I have looked for these in the archive. There are none in it -- not none catalogued, none collected, which is a stranger kind of absence than a gap.

discoveries.notes: Evolution, and the discipline Lothal never used. The section is read bottom-up by the player rather than explained; the clear-weather gate is literal -- you cannot see the graduation in flat light.

discoveries.name: Red Delta Rice, Wild
discoveries.subject: flora_red_delta_rice

levels.entry: Something red is growing out of the granary walls. Not planted, I think.
A cereal, thin-stemmed, the grain red rather than pale. It is rooted in the silt that filled the chambers, several feet above the water table.
Red Delta Rice, which the chronicles say filled these very chambers. It did not need to be reintroduced. It simply never entirely left.

It is growing where the silt is deepest, which is to say where the flood put it. The plant tolerates a salinity that would kill the pale varieties, and the granary walls have been wicking salt out of the delta for four hundred years.
If it will grow in salt, it will grow in the eastern field, which the camp has been failing to plant with the wrong crop every spring since the Shattering.
The field was never poisoned in the sense the camp means. It is salt, brought up by whatever opened underneath it, and salt is a thing some plants have already solved.
Eight acres, sown from the granary walls. It will not be a good crop for three years and it will be a crop.

discoveries.notes: The slice's central chain, and the clearest case of knowledge being help: five rungs of ordinary botany, then the field. Deliberately requires the poison discovery, so the player cannot act before they understand.

discoveries.name: The Road Still Goes the Long Way

levels.entry: The caravan road bends north here for no reason I can see, and adds half a day.
Everyone stops at the same ground, which is exposed, far from the well, and inconvenient.
Laid over the old shoreline, the bend is not a bend. The road is following a bank that has not held water in sixty years.
The camp is at a crossing. There is nothing to cross, and the caravans still stop where the ford was, because that is where you stop.

Nobody chose to keep doing this. The road is older than any of them and it remembers something none of them do -- the same sixty years the outermost seawall counts, from the other side of the argument.

discoveries.notes: The map's quietest discovery and possibly its best: habit outliving the reason for it, with nobody at fault. Moved to Dwarka with the Caravan Ground. Its last rung used to require `discovery_channel_gravel`, which retired with the Dry Harbour; it now rests on the seawall chain, which dates the sea's departure from the other direction. The transplant is close to free because the chain was always about a road outliving the water it was laid beside, and that is Dwarka's whole premise now.

discoveries.name: What the Field Gives Instead of Grain

levels.entry: The white crust on the eastern field is not all the same white. Some of it has a shine on it.
The shine gathers where the kiln ash was tipped, years ago, at the field's low corner. Nowhere else.
Ash and brine and a hot summer, and the crust there has run together into something between salt and glass. It will hold an edge for a day before it goes cloudy.
The brine is the reason nothing grows and also the reason this happens at all. The field has one thing to give and it is not a crop.
Fired properly rather than left to a hot week, it would not go cloudy. That is a kiln's work, not a summer's.
Thrali sets his nets by feel because he cannot see the channel bed through four feet of silt-water. A pane he could hold under would show him it.
The corner of the field the camp gave up on will glaze the whole delta's worth of them, and it renews every dry week for as long as the brine keeps weeping.

discoveries.notes: The glass, sourced on Lothal rather than at the Glass Scar. The plan for this chain wanted the Scar, which is on Narmada -- but all 24 existing prerequisites are within a single map, so requiring it would have been the first cross-map dependency in the game and a design decision rather than an authoring one. The eastern field already weeps brine and already has ash tipped in it, so the material was on the map the whole time. The Scar has since moved to Dwarka with the Dry Harbour's retirement, so it is still the grander version of the same fact and still on another map -- the cross-map dependency stays available to whoever decides the game should have one.

discoveries.name: Saltreed, and What It Is For
discoveries.subject: flora_saltreed

levels.entry: Reeds, shoulder-high, growing where the water is brackish enough to kill everything else.
Saltreed. The camp roofs with it, badly -- they cut it in spring because that is when they have time.
Cut after the flood rather than before it, the stems are hollow and dry hard. Cut in spring they are full of sap and rot by winter.
Uma has been re-roofing the same three kilns every year of her life for want of somebody telling her when to cut.

discoveries.notes: Small, quick, and the first time the player helps anyone. Four rungs, ending in help -- proof that the actionable rung does not require a grand chain.

discoveries.name: Three Walls Against One Sea

levels.entry: There are three seawalls here, not one. I assumed rebuilding. It is not rebuilding -- all three still stand.
Each is founded a little higher than the one seaward of it, and each is built of what was cheap that century.
The outermost stands in dry dust, and it was built to stand in surf. Nothing about it has moved; the sea did.
Roughly a hand of sea in a hundred years, if the walls were built dry-footed. Slow enough that no single person ever saw it happen.
The gate still gets swept and the seawalls still get repaired. Neither has anything left to keep out, and only one of those facts is the interesting one.

discoveries.notes: The sober counterweight. A map about a supernatural door should be clear that the thing actually destroying the place is ordinary sea-level rise. Rewritten when Dwarka was dried out: the sea left rather than the land sinking, so a rung that assumed a live tide now reads against its absence. The chain is stronger for it — a city keeping a tide schedule for water that stopped arriving is a better observation than one keeping it for water that is still there.

discoveries.name: When the Channel Runs Silver

levels.entry: Thrali says the water turns silver and that things come up when it does. I have written it down without knowing what I have written.
It does turn silver, on a still night after rain, and it is not the moon -- it happens under cloud.
The silver is a bloom, not a light. Something microscopic rising in the closed basin when the rain freshens the top of it.
The bloom brings the small fish up, and the small fish bring everything else. Thrali's grandfather knew the whole chain and expressed it in four words.

discoveries.notes: The opening hook from the design's first thirty minutes. Resolves ecologically without making the local explanation wrong -- the Kia phrase is a compressed version of the same fact.

discoveries.name: The Cut Marks Are Writing

levels.entry: Some terrace stones carry short marks on the inner face, where they would not be seen once laid.
The same marks are on the unread shelf in the archive, on material nobody has transcribed.
They are not decoration: the same short group recurs, and it recurs at the ends of courses.
Marn's word for a terrace is khet, and he says it means held water rather than step. The recurring group is two marks, and khet is two sounds.
It is a builder's tally. Course numbers and volumes, cut on the hidden face because it was working notation and was never meant to be read.
Which makes the unread shelf a set of construction records for something the University has classified as devotional, and Okhi has been dusting them for thirty years.

discoveries.notes: Linguistics, the other unused discipline. The script is mundane on purpose -- a works ledger, not a prophecy. The plateau's past is administrative, which is a truer kind of old.

discoveries.name: What the Terraces Are For

levels.entry: Stone terraces above the herders' camp. The survey calls them devotional. I have no reason yet to disagree.
Every course is lower at the outer edge. If they were built to be looked at, that is a strange way to do it.
They are not level and they are not random: the fall is consistent, about a finger in a pace, running along the hill rather than down it.
Water put on the top course would not run off. It would walk sideways across the whole hill and take a day doing it.
Marn's people graze them and have never wondered about them. They know the ground stays wet up here into the dry months and have not connected the two facts, which is fair -- neither had I.
This is irrigation, and it is enormous, and it is a farm rather than a shrine. It is also a farm for a great many more people than live on this plateau now.

discoveries.notes: The archaeology through-line. Resolves as engineering without making the herders ignorant -- they have the observation and not the question, which is the commonest way to not know something.

discoveries.name: How the Tower Sat Down
discoveries.subject: settlement_lothal

levels.entry: Twenty-two storeys in the chronicles. Four here, and a great deal of rubble that is not shaped like rubble.
The fallen stone lies in courses. It did not scatter -- it descended.
The delta took the foundation before anything took the walls. The tower sank into its own footing and the upper structure came through the lower.
Kavik built for a delta that drained. After the Shattering it stopped draining. The tower did not fail; the ground under it changed its mind.

discoveries.notes: Opens the stair shaft. The reading is deliberately sympathetic to Kavik -- the building was sound and the world moved.

discoveries.name: The Camp Can Winter Here
discoveries.subject: settlement_lothal

levels.entry: Bekh keeps a count of what the camp has and what it will need, and the two columns have never met. They move every third winter because of the gap.
The gap is not food. It is the four months when nothing can be done -- no firing, no threshing, no fishing worth the walk -- and stores go while nobody is adding to them.
Each of those four months is stopped by a different thing, and I have written down the answer to all three without noticing they were one question.
A spring kiln that fires means the glass gets made. The glass means Thrali fishes the silt-water months. The fall means the rice is threshed while the weather is against them rather than after it.

Nothing here is new. The mill is Harappan, the kiln is the camp's own, the brine has been weeping since the Shattering. All that has changed is that somebody wrote down which end of each thing the work comes out of.
Bekh went through it twice and then went quiet, and then asked whether I was sure about the kiln. She has moved this camp nine times.
They are not moving in the spring. That is the whole of it, and it is more than I came here to do.

discoveries.notes: The capstone, and deliberately not a machine. The three chains under it were each already useful alone; this is the rung where the player notices they are one system, which is the only thing being 'built'. Requires all three and is required by nothing -- the graph runs one way. Written to stay in the diary's register: the last rung is a camp not moving, not a train arriving.

discoveries.name: A Skeleton That Does Not Fit

levels.entry: A partial skeleton in the midden, picked over. Not fish, not bird, not anything I can put a name to.
The limb bones are paired the wrong way. Whatever this was did not share an ancestor with anything I have drawn on this continent.
Not deformity, and not two animals mixed: the joints articulate. It worked. Something walked around inside this.
The teeth are the argument. Replacement runs from the back forward, which nothing here does, and the wear says it lived long enough to be old.
So it did not arrive as a curiosity in somebody's cargo. It arrived, and then it lived, and then it died here and was thrown out with the fish spine.

discoveries.notes: The evolution discovery, and the one that makes the academy's answers untenable. Deliberately unglamorous -- the remarkable thing is in a rubbish heap, because that is where the city put it.

field_questions.question: Eight acres of good silt beside permanent water, and the camp has taken nothing off it in a generation. They call it poisoned. I do not think they mean anything precise by the word, and I do not yet have a better one.
field_questions.local_knowledge: The ground was spoiled in the Shattering and will come back when it chooses to.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: Contamination from below, of the kind the Narmada rift literature describes. Untreatable without instruments nobody has.

resolutions.conclusion: The field is spoiled and will not be planted again in our lifetimes.
resolutions.revisit: The granary walls are carrying more salt than the field and something is growing out of them.

resolutions.conclusion: It is salt, weeping up from whatever opened underneath. The soil is not ruined for everything -- only for what they have been planting. The rice on the granary walls has been solving this problem unsupervised for four hundred years.

field_questions.notes: The slice's proof that knowledge is help. Both readings are reasonable; only one leads to eight acres of crop, and reaching it needs botany and archaeology together.

field_questions.question: Why does the spring not match its surveyed position?

resolutions.revisit: There are three basins, in three places, built at three times. A careless surveyor does not build three.

resolutions.conclusion: The spring migrates along an opening fault, and has done so at least three times within living memory.

field_questions.local_knowledge: Marn's grandmother named a year for it. The herders rebuilt the catch basin twice and did not think this remarkable enough to mention to anyone at the University, who did not ask.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: A fixed spring, surveyed once in 371 and never resurveyed, since springs do not move. The archive is internally consistent and has simply never been checked against the hill.
field_questions.notes: The forgiving reading -- blaming the surveyor -- is the wrong one, and it is wrong in the direction the player will be tempted by after Lothal. Being anti-academy is not the same as being right either.

field_questions.question: The fisher tells me the channel runs silver and that the creatures rise when it does. He offers this as a fact about the world and not as a puzzle. I cannot decide whether the silver brings them or whether both follow from something I have not seen.
field_questions.local_knowledge: Thal-uvai: the water remembers. Said of the basin on still nights after rain, and of two or three other things.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: Lunar tidal influence on a closed basin, per the Narmada literature on coastal anomalies.

resolutions.conclusion: The moon draws the water and the water draws the creatures, as the University would have it.
resolutions.revisit: It happens under heavy cloud and at every phase. Whatever the moon is doing, it is not this.

resolutions.conclusion: A bloom rises in the closed basin when rain freshens its surface; the small fish follow the bloom and everything else follows the small fish. The Kia phrase says the same thing in four words and does not pretend to a mechanism.

field_questions.notes: The opening question. The academic reading is available first and is wrong, which is the point: the player should be able to close the entry early and be mistaken.

field_questions.question: What are the terraces above the herders' camp for?

resolutions.conclusion: A devotional feature, as the University survey records.
resolutions.revisit: The marks are cut on the inner faces, where nothing meant to be seen would put them.

resolutions.conclusion: Grazing platforms cut by the herders' own ancestors.
resolutions.revisit: The fall runs along the hill rather than down it. Nobody levels two hundred courses for goats.

resolutions.conclusion: Contour irrigation on a scale requiring a population the archive has no record of.

field_questions.local_knowledge: Marn's people graze them, maintain the odd fallen course out of habit, and have no account of who built them. They will tell you the ground up there stays wet, and offer it as a fact about the ground.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: The survey of 388 assigns them a devotional function on the grounds of scale and effort, reasoning that no agricultural return could justify the labour. The reasoning is sound and the premise -- that the population was the present population -- is assumed rather than established.
field_questions.notes: Two wrong readings rather than one, and the second is the sympathetic error: crediting the locals is not the same as being right about them.

field_questions.question: Is the grey scarp-bird one species or two?

resolutions.conclusion: Two closely related species, as the archive's two entries record.
resolutions.revisit: The heavy-billed ones are all old ones. The bill does not stop growing when the bird does.

resolutions.conclusion: One species. The bill grows throughout life, and the two entries are a young bird and an old one, catalogued sixty years apart by observers who never read each other.

field_questions.local_knowledge: Marn has one word for the bird and another for an old one, in the way one has a word for a colt and a horse. He is surprised the question is a question.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: Two species, on the authority of two independent careful descriptions. No mechanism exists in the University for a catalogue entry to be revisited, so the duplication is invisible from inside.
field_questions.notes: The binomial contradiction the two repos actually had, written into the fiction. The sound reading needs the quarry section because it takes seeing graduated forms in the rock to accept a graduated form in the air.

field_questions.question: There are animals in this midden that belong to no lineage on this continent, at a city whose people say a door opens in the mist. I have three respectable explanations and I am losing confidence in all of them.

resolutions.conclusion: Vagrants and escaped stock from a trading city, misremembered into a story about a door.
resolutions.revisit: Nine layers, over four hundred years, of animals that share no ancestor with anything on this coast. Trade does not do that, and it does not do it in clusters.

resolutions.conclusion: A relict population from before the Shattering, surviving in the drowned quarter and coming ashore.
resolutions.revisit: A relict lineage would still be a lineage. These share no ancestor with anything here, and no two layers share one with each other.

resolutions.conclusion: They cross. The gate is real, it is not rare, and the people who live beside it have been correct about it for four hundred years while being unable to say why.

field_questions.local_knowledge: Sura will tell you the gate opens in mist, that you sweep after, and that the bones go in the midden with everything else. She is not being mystical. She is telling you the procedure, the way you would explain bins.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: The Narmada position is that Dwarka is a trading port with an old story and poor record-keeping, and that every specimen produced so far has been either a misidentified juvenile or a hoax. No scholar has been to the midden.
field_questions.notes: The map's thesis, and the one question in the game where the local account is simply correct and the academy simply wrong. Both wrong readings are respectable and one of them is what a good naturalist would reach for second.

field_questions.question: The city is being lost. I would like to be able to say to somebody in authority what is losing it, and I notice I want the answer to be the interesting one.

resolutions.conclusion: The gate. Whatever comes through is taking the place apart by degrees.
resolutions.revisit: Three walls, sixty years of toll ledgers, and a hand of sea a century. Nothing that came through the court has moved a single course of stone.

resolutions.conclusion: The sea, rising slowly enough that no one person has ever watched it happen, and no more mysterious than that.

field_questions.local_knowledge: Pell has rebuilt the inner wall once in his life and expects his son to do it again. He does not connect that to anything; it is simply what the wall is for.
field_questions.academic_hypothesis: The survey of 402 records the Dwarka coastline as stable, on the basis of a single visit and the outermost wall being described as a breakwater.
field_questions.notes: The counterweight question, and the one where the player's own appetite for a good story is the thing being tested. The unsound reading is the one this map has spent the whole time making attractive.

vocabulary.notes: A stratigraphic term in a language with no word for stratigraphy. The bone-pickers needed to tell each other which layer they meant.

vocabulary.literal: A prefix rather than a word. Attaches to what the water is holding: thal-uvai, water holding memory; thal-set, water holding a path.
vocabulary.notes: The key that opens the Kia readings. Thrali has half of it; Bekh supplies the rest by using it without explaining.

vocabulary.literal: Water that holds a way through it. Said of the marsh between the pale mangroves.
vocabulary.notes: Names the channel before the player can see it, which is the point -- the language encodes the ecology.
Completes thal-uvai. Compresses an entire trophic chain into a phrase that sounds like superstition.
Distinguishes the mist that does something from the mist that does not, which is a distinction the University has no vocabulary for and no reason to want.
A year-name rather than a date. Evidence the archive cannot accept, because its form is a story.
The word that turns two hundred courses of stone from ornament into engineering. The herders kept the meaning inside the noun for long enough that nobody had to remember it.
Two words for one animal at two ages, which is a more accurate taxonomy than the archive's two species and was never intended as one.
